newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE central bank head wants exchange commission.
newsitem.headline: UAE central bank head wants exchange commission.

text.p: United Arab Emirates (UAE) central bank governor Sultan Nasser al-Suweidi on Sunday called for the creation of a stock exchange commission to oversee a future official stock market in the Gulf Arab state.

"Establishing a separate regulatory body is paramount to ensuring the future success of the UAE stock exchange...What is needed is a UAE Stock Exchange Commission," Suweidi told a gathering of bankers and investment houses in Abu Dhabi.
The Commission and the exchange's own regulatory body would work to protect investors by policing against insider dealing, market manipulation and guaranteeing financial disclosure.
"Both must work to prohibit insider abuses, market manipulation and other injustices in the market," he said.
"To protect the market, the exchange must police and discipline itself and be subject to policing and discipline by the commission," Suweidi added.

The UAE has no formal stock market but shares of 27 local firms are traded informally through a handful of brokers. Shares are only open to UAE nationals and company disclosure levels are not as high as in Western equity markets.
A draft law on the creation of a formal exchange in the oil-rich country would be issued this year, Suweidi said.
Drawing up market regulations, deciding on the extent of foreign ownership allowed and where to locate the exchange have so far delayed the long-planned establishment of a bourse.

Regulations should cover trader conduct, insider dealing, position financing limit, investor margin credit and foreign participation, Jaafar Badwan, a manager at the government-owned Abu Dhabi Investment Co told the conference.
Suweidi said no decision had yet been made on the number or location of trading floors but confirmed that foreign investment would be permitted.

"The market can be anywhere...It doesn't have to be one place. It depends on where there is a critical mass of companies...We have suggested that a certain percentage of foreign ownership should be allowed," Suweidi said.

Trading floors in Abu Dhabi and the neighbouring emirate of Dubai would be electronically linked with foreign firms initially allowed to hold 10 percent of shares, an official at Dubai's economic department said last year.
